title: 📘 UNIT 5: GEOGRAPHY AND ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT
notes: Geographic location influences economic development through geology, relief, climate, soils, biodiversity, transportation and access to markets.

title: 🌍 5.1 EFFECTS OF GEOGRAPHIC LOCATION ON DEVELOPMENT
notes:
Geographic location affects where economic activities occur and how easily goods, people and services move.

Important geographical influences :-
🔹 Climate
🔹 Relief and topography
🔹 Soil
🔹 Natural resources
🔹 Distance from markets
🔹 Transportation networks
🔹 Access to the sea
🔹 Population distribution

⭐ Geographic location influences agricultural, industrial and commercial development.

title: 🗺️ 5.1.1 GEOGRAPHIC DETERMINISM
notes:
Geographic determinism :- the idea that physical geography strongly determines the economic and social development of societies.

🔹 Climate, terrain, natural resources and location are viewed as major forces shaping human development.

Important proponents discussed include :-
👤 Karl Ritter
👤 Ellen Churchill Semple
👤 Ellsworth Huntington

⚠️ Limitation :- it can underestimate human creativity, technology and the ability of societies to modify environmental conditions.

title: 🧠 5.1.2 POSSIBILISM
notes:
Possibilism :- the view that the environment provides opportunities and limitations, but human beings can use technology, knowledge and creativity to modify their environment.

Important proponents :-
👤 Lucien Paul Victor Febvre
👤 Paul Vidal de la Blache

⭐ Key idea :- “Nature is never more than an adviser.”

Technology allows societies to overcome or reduce some geographical limitations.

title: 🌾 5.1.3 LOCATION AND AGRICULTURAL DEVELOPMENT
notes:
Agricultural production and profitability depend partly on the suitability of land and environmental resources.

👤 Johann Heinrich von Thünen developed the agricultural location theory in 1826 in “The Isolated State.”

His model assumes :-
🔹 A self-sufficient isolated state.
🔹 A central market city.
🔹 Uniform physical conditions.
🔹 Equal rationality among farmers.
🔹 Transport costs increase with distance from the market.
🔹 Land rent increases toward the market.

⭐ Main principle :- distance from the market influences the type and intensity of agricultural production.

title: ⭕ 5.1.3.1 VON THÜNEN'S CONCENTRIC LAND-USE MODEL
notes:
Four major agricultural zones around the central market are proposed :-

🥬 Zone 1 :- intensive farming, dairying, vegetables, fruits and other perishable products.

🌳 Zone 2 :- forest products such as firewood and timber.

🌾 Zone 3 :- extensive field crops such as grains.

🐄 Zone 4 :- animal ranching; animals can transport themselves toward the market.

🌲 Beyond the fourth zone :- wilderness/unused land because of the great distance from the market.

⭐ Heavy and perishable goods tend to be produced closer to markets because transportation is costly.

title: 🏭 5.1.4 LOCATION AND INDUSTRIAL DEVELOPMENT
notes:
Industrial location depends on :-
🔹 Raw materials
🔹 Labour
🔹 Transportation costs
🔹 Energy
🔹 Markets
🔹 Consumers
🔹 Agglomeration economies

👤 Alfred Weber developed the Least-Cost Industrial Location Theory.

⭐ Main objective :- locate industries where total costs are minimized and profits can be maximized.

title: 🔺 5.1.4.1 WEBER'S LEAST-COST THEORY
notes:
Weber identified three major influences on industrial location :-

🚚 Transportation costs
👷 Labour costs
🏙️ Agglomeration economies

Transportation was considered the most important component.

📐 Location Triangle :- represents the relationship between the factory, market and sources of raw materials.

⭐ Firms seek locations that minimize the combined cost of moving raw materials and finished products.

title: ⚖️ 5.1.4.2 WEIGHT-LOSING AND WEIGHT-GAINING INDUSTRIES
notes:
📉 Weight-losing industry :- the finished product weighs less than the raw materials used.

Examples :-
🔹 Bauxite and iron-ore processing
🔹 Steel production
🔹 Sugar-cane mills

➡️ These industries tend to locate near raw-material sources.

📈 Weight-gaining industry :- the finished product becomes heavier or bulkier during production.

Examples :-
🔹 Cotton textiles
🔹 Soft-drink bottling
🔹 Breweries
🔹 Beverage industries

➡️ These industries tend to locate closer to markets.

⭐ Material Index (MI) = Weight of Inputs ÷ Weight of Outputs

MI > 1 :- locate closer to raw materials.
MI < 1 :- locate closer to the market.

title: 🏙️ 5.1.5 LOCATION AND SETTLEMENT / SERVICE-CENTER DEVELOPMENT
notes:
👤 Walter Christaller developed Central Place Theory in 1933 after studying settlement patterns in southern Germany.

Central place :- a settlement or nodal point that supplies surrounding areas with goods and services.

⭐ Main concepts :-
🎯 Centrality :- attraction or importance of a particular center.
👥 Threshold :- minimum population/purchasing power required to support a service.
📏 Range :- maximum distance consumers are willing to travel for goods or services.

title: ⬡ 5.1.5.1 CHRISTALLER'S CENTRAL PLACE THEORY
notes:
Christaller proposed a hierarchical settlement system based on hexagonal market areas.

Three principles :-
1️⃣ Marketing Principle :- K = 3
2️⃣ Transportation Principle :- K = 4
3️⃣ Administrative Principle :- K = 7

🏙️ Higher-order centers :- provide more specialized and higher-order goods/services.
🏘️ Lower-order centers :- provide everyday goods and basic services.

⭐ Hexagons reduce overlapping market areas better than circular market areas.

title: ⚠️ 5.1.5.2 LIMITATIONS OF LOCATION THEORIES
notes:
The models of von Thünen, Weber and Christaller make simplified assumptions.

Limitations include :-
🔹 Uniform physical landscapes are unrealistic.
🔹 Transport systems are diverse rather than uniform.
🔹 Markets are influenced by many external factors.
🔹 Consumer purchasing power is not equal everywhere.
🔹 Government policies influence location.
🔹 Technology changes transportation and production costs.

⭐ Despite limitations, the theories remain important for understanding spatial organization of economic activities.

title: 🌡️ 5.2 CLIMATE EXTREMES AND POVERTY
notes:
Extreme climate refers to climatic or weather conditions that exceed normal thresholds for a particular place and period.

Examples :-
🔥 Extreme heat
❄️ Extreme cold
🌧️ Extreme rainfall
🌊 Floods
🏜️ Droughts
🌪️ Storms and tornadoes
🦗 Plagues associated with environmental extremes

⭐ Climate extremes can reduce agricultural production, damage assets and increase poverty.

title: 🔗 5.2.1 CLIMATE CHANGE–POVERTY LINKAGE
notes:
Poor households are often more vulnerable to climate extremes because they have fewer assets and weaker coping capacity.

Climate extremes can cause :-
🌾 Crop losses
🐄 Livestock losses
🏠 Housing destruction
💧 Water shortages
🏥 Health problems
📚 Disruption of education
💰 Loss of income

⭐ Poverty also increases environmental pressure because poor households may depend heavily on natural resources for survival.

This can create a vicious cycle :-
Climate extremes → livelihood losses → poverty → reduced coping capacity → greater vulnerability.

title: 🏜️ 5.2.2 DROUGHT AND POVERTY
notes:
Drought :- an extended period of unusually low precipitation causing water shortages.

Major effects :-
🌾 Reduced crop yields
🐄 Livestock deaths
💧 Water scarcity
🍚 Food insecurity
💰 Income losses
🏚️ Loss of household assets

⭐ Repeated droughts can force poor households to sell productive assets, weakening their ability to recover from future shocks.

title: 🌊 5.2.3 FLOODING EVENTS AND POVERTY
notes:
Floods can damage both rural livelihoods and urban infrastructure.

Major effects :-
🌾 Destruction of crops
🐄 Livestock losses
🏠 Damage to homes
🛣️ Damage to roads and infrastructure
💧 Damage to water and power systems
👥 Displacement
🍚 Food insecurity
💰 Loss of income and property

🇪🇹 Ethiopia example :- flooding along the Baro River in Gambella has affected agropastoral households through crop, livestock and property losses.

⭐ Preventive measures include moving livestock/property, harvesting early, digging ditches, raising house floors and constructing boundary walls.

title: 🔒 5.2.4 POVERTY TRAPS AND CRITICAL THRESHOLDS
notes:
Poverty trap :- a situation where repeated climate shocks push poor households into deeper and persistent poverty.

🔄 Typical cycle :-
Climate shock → asset loss → reduced income → selling remaining assets → weaker coping capacity → deeper poverty → greater vulnerability.

Critical threshold :- a point at which repeated damage causes severe or difficult-to-reverse losses.

⭐ Repeated droughts, floods and famines can weaken social networks, assets and human capital.

title: 🌍 5.2.5 GEOGRAPHY OF CLIMATE EXTREMES AND POVERTY
notes:
The textbook identifies Sub-Saharan Africa, South Asia and Southeast Asia as areas where high poverty levels overlap with significant climate risks.

🔹 Tropical areas are particularly vulnerable to climate extremes.
🔹 Changes in temperature and rainfall can affect agriculture and livelihoods.
🔹 Poor households have limited resources for adaptation.

⭐ Disaster-risk reduction should therefore be an important part of poverty-reduction and development strategies.

title: 🚢 5.3 DISADVANTAGES OF LANDLOCKED COUNTRIES
notes:
Landlocked countries :- countries without direct access to the sea.

🌍 There are more than 30 landlocked countries worldwide.

Major disadvantages :-
🚚 High transportation costs
🛃 Dependence on transit countries
⏳ Long transit delays
💰 Additional customs and transit charges
🛣️ Dependence on foreign infrastructure
⚔️ Vulnerability to political conflicts
🚧 Border closures

🇪🇹 Ethiopia is a major example of a landlocked country.

title: 🚚 5.3.1 TRANSPORTATION CHALLENGES OF LANDLOCKED COUNTRIES
notes:
Landlocked countries depend on neighboring transit countries to reach international ports.

Challenges include :-
🔹 Poor transport infrastructure
🔹 Long distances to ports
🔹 Border delays
🔹 Customs procedures
🔹 Transit fees
🔹 Road and railway limitations
🔹 Seasonal disruption

⭐ Transportation costs make imports more expensive and can reduce the competitiveness of exports.

title: 🛃 5.3.2 TRANSIT AND CUSTOMS BARRIERS
notes:
Transit-related costs may include :-

🔹 Transit licenses
🔹 Border fees
🔹 Temporary road licenses
🔹 Foreign vehicle permits
🔹 Toll charges
🔹 Customs verification fees
🔹 Security bonds
🔹 Police and escort charges

⏳ Border crossings in Africa can involve delays of 24–48 hours and sometimes much longer.

⭐ Administrative burdens increase the cost and time of international trade.

title: ⚔️ 5.3.3 POLITICAL CHALLENGES OF LANDLOCKED COUNTRIES
notes:
Landlocked countries are vulnerable to political conditions in transit neighbors.

Possible problems :-
🔹 Border closures
🔹 Civil conflict
🔹 Political instability
🔹 Loss of access rights
🔹 Weak negotiating capacity
🔹 Disrupted trade corridors

🇪🇹 Ethiopia :- the conflict with Eritrea after 1997 prevented Ethiopia from using the ports of Assab and Massawa. Ethiopia subsequently relied heavily on Djibouti for transit trade.

⭐ Good political relations with transit neighbors are essential for reliable trade.

title: 🌍 5.3.4 ETHIOPIA AND LANDLOCKEDNESS
notes:
Ethiopia has no seaport and depends heavily on neighboring countries for international trade.

Major routes discussed include :-
🇩🇯 Djibouti
🇸🇩 Sudan
🇰🇪 Kenya
🇸🇴 Somalia

Challenges :-
🔹 Limited transport networks
🔹 High transport costs
🔹 Dependence on transit countries
🔹 Border delays
🔹 Political instability along alternative routes

⭐ Ethiopia's landlocked position has a significant effect on its international trade and economic development.

title: 🤝 5.3.5 STRATEGIES FOR LANDLOCKED COUNTRIES
notes:
Possible ways to reduce landlocked disadvantages :-

🛣️ Improve roads, railways and transport networks.
🤝 Strengthen relations with transit neighbors.
🛃 Simplify customs procedures.
📑 Reduce unnecessary administrative charges.
🚢 Develop reliable access to multiple ports.
🌍 Strengthen regional integration.
📦 Improve logistics and supply chains.

⭐ Regional cooperation can reduce the economic disadvantages caused by lack of direct sea access.

title: 🌍 5.4 INTRAREGIONAL TRADE IN AFRICA
notes:
Intraregional trade :- exchange of goods and services among countries within the same region.

Africa's growing population, rising incomes and urbanization are increasing demand for food and consumer goods.

⭐ African trade pattern is characterized by :-
🔹 Significant imports of processed food products.
🔹 Exports often dominated by untreated or less-processed products.
🔹 Growing potential for intra-African agricultural trade.
🔹 Regional integration efforts through Regional Economic Communities.

title: 🌾 5.4.1 INTRA-AFRICAN AGRICULTURAL TRADE
notes:
Intra-African agricultural exports have increased since 2000.

Regional Economic Communities (RECs) promote regional trade through preferential tariffs, free-trade arrangements and customs unions.

Major RECs discussed :-
🌍 AMU :- Arab Maghreb Union
🌍 COMESA :- Common Market for Eastern and Southern Africa
🌍 ECOWAS :- Economic Community of West African States
🌍 SADC :- Southern African Development Community

⭐ Agricultural trade within Africa provides opportunities for food markets and regional economic integration.

title: 📈 5.4.2 TRADE FLOW TRENDS
notes:
The value of intra-African food and agricultural trade generally increased over the period discussed in the textbook.

📊 Key points :-
🔹 Trade rose substantially from the late 2000s.
🔹 It peaked around 2013.
🔹 A decline followed before trade resumed an upward trend around 2016.
🔹 Intra-continental agricultural exports grew faster than extra-continental exports during part of the period.

⭐ SADC and COMESA countries were major contributors to intra-African agricultural exports.

title: 🏆 5.4.3 TOP EXPORTERS AND IMPORTERS
notes:
South Africa remained the dominant intra-African agricultural exporter in the period covered by the textbook.

Important exporters include :-
🇿🇦 South Africa
🇪🇬 Egypt
🇺🇬 Uganda
🇰🇪 Kenya
🇹🇿 Tanzania

Important importers include :-
🇿🇦 South Africa
🇰🇪 Kenya
🇪🇬 Egypt
🇿🇼 Zimbabwe
🇲🇿 Mozambique
🇨🇩 Democratic Republic of Congo

⭐ Eastern and Southern African and Maghreb countries play major roles in intra-African agricultural trade.

title: 🌾 5.4.4 COMMODITY COMPOSITION OF TRADE FLOWS
notes:
Important agricultural products traded within Africa include :-

🌽 Maize
🌾 Wheat
🍚 Rice
🐄 Cattle
🍎 Fruits
🥬 Vegetables
☕ Coffee
🍵 Tea
🌴 Palm oil
🌿 Cotton
🍬 Sweeteners
🥤 Beverages
🍱 Processed foods

⭐ Intra-African agricultural trade is more diversified than trade in some other developing regions.

title: 🚧 5.4.5 INTRA-AFRICAN TRADE POLICIES AND CHALLENGES
notes:
Major barriers include :-

💰 Tariff barriers :- taxes or duties imposed on imported goods.

📑 Non-tariff measures :- regulations, procedures and administrative requirements that restrict trade.

🚧 Other challenges :-
🔹 Poor transport infrastructure
🔹 Border delays
🔹 Administrative barriers
🔹 Weak production capacity
🔹 Limited processing industries
🔹 Informal trade
🔹 Currency problems
🔹 Political instability

⭐ Non-tariff barriers can sometimes restrict trade more strongly than tariffs.

title: 💱 5.4.6 INFORMAL CROSS-BORDER TRADE
notes:
Informal cross-border trade occurs outside formal trade channels or official procedures.

🇪🇹 Ethiopia case :- informal currency exchange may use prevailing black-market exchange rates when traders agree on prices in different currencies.

Problems associated with informal trade :-
🔹 Loss of government revenue
🔹 Unofficial exchange rates
🔹 Unrecorded trade flows
🔹 Unfavorable terms of trade
🔹 Foreign-currency shortages

⭐ Informal trade also shows how excessive formal barriers can encourage traders to avoid official channels.

title: 🔗 5.4.7 REGIONAL VALUE CHAINS
notes:
Regional value chains connect producers, processors, transporters, traders and consumers across countries.

To strengthen African value chains, the textbook emphasizes :-
🛣️ Better roads
🚚 Better transport
📡 Better information systems
🏭 Agro-processing facilities
🤝 Stronger links between producers and markets
🛒 Better access to cross-border markets

⭐ Developing regional value chains can increase trade, processing, employment and food-market opportunities.

title: 🧠 UNIT 5 KEY CONCEPTS
notes:
🌍 Geographic location :- position of a place and its relationship with physical, economic and human systems.

🧭 Geographic determinism :- environment strongly determines human and economic development.

🧠 Possibilism :- humans can use technology and creativity to modify environmental opportunities and limitations.

🌾 von Thünen :- agricultural location theory.

🏭 Alfred Weber :- least-cost industrial location theory.

🏙️ Walter Christaller :- central place theory.

📉 Weight-losing industry :- finished product weighs less than raw materials.

📈 Weight-gaining industry :- finished product becomes heavier/bulkier.

📐 Material Index :- weight of inputs ÷ weight of outputs.

⬡ Central place :- settlement providing goods and services to surrounding areas.

👥 Threshold :- minimum purchasing power/population required to support a service.

📏 Range :- maximum distance consumers travel for a good or service.

🌡️ Climate extreme :- climatic condition exceeding normal thresholds.

🔒 Poverty trap :- repeated shocks push poor households into persistent poverty.

🚢 Landlocked country :- country without direct access to the sea.

🌍 Intraregional trade :- trade among countries within the same region.

💰 Tariff :- tax or duty on imported goods.

📑 Non-tariff measure :- non-tax regulation or administrative barrier affecting trade.

🤝 Regional Economic Community :- regional organization promoting economic cooperation and integration.

title: ⭐ UNIT 5 QUICK REVISION
notes:
📌 Geographic location influences agriculture, industry, settlements and trade.

📌 Geographic determinism emphasizes the influence of physical geography on development.

📌 Possibilism emphasizes human ability to overcome geographical limitations.

📌 von Thünen explained agricultural land-use patterns according to distance from markets and transport costs.

📌 von Thünen's four major zones progress from intensive farming/dairying to forest products, field crops and animal ranching.

📌 Weber's least-cost theory focuses on transportation, labour and agglomeration economies.

📌 Material Index > 1 → industry should locate nearer the raw-material source.

📌 Material Index < 1 → industry should locate nearer the market.

📌 Christaller's Central Place Theory explains hierarchical settlements and service centers.

📌 Christaller's three principles :- K=3 Marketing, K=4 Transportation, K=7 Administrative.

📌 Climate extremes can destroy crops, livestock, property, income and infrastructure.

📌 Repeated climate shocks can create poverty traps by reducing assets and coping capacity.

📌 Landlocked countries face high transport costs, transit dependence, border delays and political risks.

📌 Ethiopia depends heavily on Djibouti and other neighboring countries for access to international trade routes.

📌 Intraregional trade means trade among countries within Africa.

📌 AMU, COMESA, ECOWAS and SADC are important Regional Economic Communities.

📌 South Africa is a major intra-African agricultural exporter.

📌 Tariff and non-tariff barriers are major obstacles to formal intra-African trade.

📌 Better roads, transport, information systems and agro-processing can strengthen African regional value chains.

⭐ Core idea :- Geography creates opportunities and constraints for development, while technology, policies, infrastructure and regional cooperation can reduce geographical barriers.
